## Proof

**Claim:** The Laplace transform is **not injective** on the class of piecewise continuous functions on $[0, \infty)$. Specifically, $(\mathcal{L}f)(s) = 0$ for all $s \in \mathbb{R}^+$ does **not** imply $f(t) = 0$ for all $t \geq 0$.

**Construction.** Define

$$f(t) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } t = 1, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$

**Step 1: $f$ is piecewise continuous.** On any finite interval $[0, N]$, the function $f$ has exactly one discontinuity (at $t = 1$). At this point, the one-sided limits exist and are finite:

$$\lim_{t \to 1^-} f(t) = 0, \qquad \lim_{t \to 1^+} f(t) = 0.$$

The function is continuous everywhere else. Hence $f$ is piecewise continuous on $[0, \infty)$.

**Step 2: $(\mathcal{L}f)(s) = 0$ for all $s > 0$.** The Laplace transform is

$$(\mathcal{L}f)(s) = \int_0^\infty f(t)\, e^{-st}\, dt.$$

Since $f(t) = 0$ for all $t \neq 1$, the integrand $f(t)e^{-st}$ is zero everywhere except possibly at the single point $t = 1$. A Riemann (or Lebesgue) integral over an interval is unaffected by the value of the integrand at any single point—changing a function at one point does not change its integral. Therefore

$$(\mathcal{L}f)(s) = \int_0^\infty f(t)\, e^{-st}\, dt = 0 \qquad \text{for all } s > 0.$$

**Step 3: $f$ is not identically zero.** By construction, $f(1) = 1 \neq 0$.

**Conclusion.** We have exhibited a piecewise continuous function $f$ with $(\mathcal{L}f)(s) = 0$ for all $s \in \mathbb{R}^+$, yet $f \not\equiv 0$. Therefore the Laplace transform is **not injective** on the class of piecewise continuous functions.

**Remark.** The obstruction is fundamental: the Laplace transform is defined by an integral, and integrals are insensitive to values on sets of measure zero. Any piecewise continuous function that differs from zero only at isolated points (or more generally on a measure-zero set) will have a vanishing Laplace transform without being identically zero. Injectivity can be restored only by identifying functions that agree almost everywhere (i.e., working in $L^1_{\text{loc}}$), or by restricting to a class where point values are determined by the surrounding behavior—such as continuous functions, where Lerch's theorem guarantees injectivity.
